80652267.title: 2011 Flat Rock–Trenton tornado
80652267.extract:
On the afternoon of April 27, 2011, a large, long-tracked, and destructive high-end EF4 tornado, known informally as the Section–Flat Rock EF4 by the National Weather Service, moved across portions of North Alabama and North Georgia, tracking near the towns of Section, Pisgah, Flat Rock, Higdon and Rosalie in Alabama and Trenton in Georgia along its 47-mile-long (76 km) track. The tornado directly killed 15 people, injured at least 50 more, and impacted hundreds of structures. It occurred as part of the largest tornado outbreak in modern history, and was one of multiple EF4-rated tornadoes to be confirmed that day. 
The tornado first touched down near Section, initially producing EF0 and EF1-rated damage to trees and homes before becoming violent north of Pisgah. Several homes were heavily damaged in the area and trees were blown down; the tornado killed 13 people in Jackson County alone. The tornado maintained its intensity as it moved through Dekalb County before crossing into Dade County, Georgia at EF4 intensity, where two people would be killed and heavy damage was inflicted to the community of Trenton. The tornado lifted after 56 minutes on the ground. Damage from the tornado was rated EF4 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, and damage surveyors estimated that the tornado had maximum estimated wind speeds of approximately 190 miles per hour (310 km/h). WDEF-TV described the tornado as the "longest-running in our area". 


== Meteorological synopsis ==


=== Setup ===
The environmental conditions leading up to the 2011 Super Outbreak were among the "most conducive to violent tornadoes ever documented". On April 25, a vigorous upper-level shortwave trough moved into the Southern Plains states. Ample instability, low-level moisture, and wind shear all fueled a significant tornado outbreak from Texas to Tennessee; at least 64 tornadoes touched down on this day. An area of low pressure consolidated over Texas on April 26 and traveled east while the aforementioned shortwave trough traversed the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys. Another 50 tornadoes touched down on this day. The multi-day outbreak culminated on April 27 with the most violent day of tornadic activity since the 1974 Super Outbreak. Multiple episodes of tornadic activity ensued with two waves of mesoscale convective systems in the morning hours followed by a widespread outbreak of supercells from Mississippi to North Carolina during the afternoon into the evening.
Tornadic activity on April 27 was precipitated by a 995 mbar (hPa; 29.39 inHg) surface low situated over Kentucky and a deep, negatively tilted (aligned northwest to southeast) trough over Arkansas and Louisiana. A strong southwesterly surface jet intersected these systems at a 60° angle, an ageostrophic flow that led to storm-relative helicity values in excess of 500 m2s−2—indicative of extreme wind shear and a very high potential for rotating updrafts within supercells. Ample moisture from the Gulf of Mexico was brought north across the Deep South, leading to daytime high temperatures of 77 to 81 °F (25 to 27 °C) and dewpoints of 66 to 72 °F (19 to 22 °C). Furthermore, convective available potential energy (CAPE) values reached 2,500–3,000 J/kg−1.


=== Forecast ===

On the morning of April 27, a strong cold front with several areas of embedded low pressure extended from the Texas Hill Country northeastward towards the Arklatex and the Ozarks, and later into the lower Ohio Valley. Warm moist air was in place due to strong southerly flow ahead of the front over Mississippi, Alabama, and Tennessee. An upper level disturbance sparked a broad area of showers and thunderstorms as it moved across the frontal boundary on the previous evening. The eastern edge of the line of showers and storms continued to move eastward, in concert with the upper disturbance, reaching the northwest Alabama border around 2:00 a.m. CDT.
This produced the last and most violent round of severe weather, which began around 2:30 p.m. CDT for northern Alabama as supercells began to line up to the southwest of the area. During the early afternoon hours, the potential for destructive tornadoes was highlighted by the Storm Prediction Center's upgrade to a high risk for severe weather around 1:00 p.m. CDT. This prompted a particularly dangerous situation (PDS) tornado watch, which was issued for northern Alabama and portions of southern Tennessee at 1:45 p.m. CDT. The bulletin that accompanied the watch read:

THE NWS STORM PREDICTION CENTER HAS ISSUED A TORNADO WATCH FOR PORTIONS OF: MUCH OF ALABAMA, NORTHWEST GEORGIA, SOUTHEAST MISSISSIPPI, SOUTHERN MIDDLE TENNESSEE, EFFECTIVE THIS WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON AND EVENING FROM 145 PM UNTIL 1000 PM CDT.
...THIS IS A PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS SITUATION...

DESTRUCTIVE TORNADOES...LARGE HAIL TO 4 INCHES IN DIAMETER. THUNDERSTORM WIND GUSTS TO 80 MPH...AND DANGEROUS LIGHTNING ARE POSSIBLE IN THESE AREAS.
The potential for tornadoes ramped up from noon through 9:00 p.m. CDT. During this period, much of Alabama experienced numerous supercell thunderstorms that produced numerous tornadoes, including the Trenton tornado.


=== Morning EF1 tornado in Trenton and New England, Georgia ===
On the morning of April 27, an EF1 tornado touched down a short distance to the north of where the EF4 tornado would later impact. The tornado touched down at around 8:40 a.m. CDT on top of an interchange in the western portions, moving to the northeast. West of Wolverine Drive the tornado reached EF1 intensity, impacting the Dade Elementary before crossing 1st Street and John Street. It weakened to EF0 strength shortly before passing over Wren Avenue. The tornado moved through a neighborhood between North Main Street and Interstate 59 before moving directly parallel to Highway 11. It reached EF1 intensity for a second  time as it impacted the northwest portions of New England, before weakening again as it crossed Squirrel Town Creek. The tornado continued northeast through unpopulated areas in Dade County to the west of Morganville. It remained relatively thin as it moved over the Slygo Ridge, part of the Slygo Valley region. Several roads were hit at EF0 intensity as the tornado continued, eventually crossing Interstate 24 and lifting a short distance to the west of Hooker. The tornado caused no fatalities or injuries.


== Tornado summary ==
This multiple-vortex EF4 tornado that originated from the Cullman supercell, with maximum sustained winds of up to 190 mph (310 km/h), devastated portions of Jackson and DeKalb counties in Alabama, as well as Dade and Walker counties in Georgia along a 47-mile-long (76 km) path at times up to 1,260 yards (1,150 m) wide, killing 14 people and injuring at least 50 others.

The tornado first touched down on Alabama State Highway 35, moving to the northeast. It moved parallel to County Road 390, before crossing over Alabama State Highway 40. Trees were blown down north of County Road 224, before the tornado briefly moved over an offshoot of the Tennessee River. It continued moving northeast through hilly areas of Marshall County, continuing to produce tree damage and damaging several homes near County Road 88. Off Alabama State Highway 88, several homes sustained damage and trees were blown down on the properties. The tornado then crossed County Road 432 and County Road 57, impacting the Dogwood Branch of the Tennessee River directly north of Pisgah. On County Roads 369, several homes were heavily damaged.
To their north the tornado tossed debris into a grove of trees and scattered debris from a property across a field. The tornado then passed over County Road 58 and County Road 357, where more damage was done to trees and homes. A home was destroyed as the tornado passed over County Road 58 before the tornado crossed over the Rocky Branch of the Tennessee River. It then impacted County Road 426 and County Road 126 north of the communities of Glenzaida and Rosalie. The tornado continued moving through areas a short distance south of the Coon Gulf and northwest to north of County Road 78. The tornado rapidly intensified to low-end EF4 strength in this area as it destroyed numerous mobile homes and brick-foundation homes, scattering debris hundreds of yards and killing three people.

Thousands of trees were snapped and debarked, vehicles were thrown up to 50 yards (46 m) in different directions, and barns and chicken houses were heavily damaged, along with the roof of a church. As it passed near Flat Rock and Higdon, the tornado reached high-end EF4 strength, mowing down thousands of trees in this rural area. As the tornado struck a farm, a home and two chicken houses were completely obliterated and swept away. A heavy propane tank was lofted and thrown 100 yards (91 m) from one of the chicken houses, and 19 cattle on the property were killed. Remarkably, a family of four taking shelter inside the house were completely unharmed. Three people were killed in a home southwest of Flat Rock. The Shiloh Community Church in the Higdon area was hit by the tornado; the same church would be struck by another tornado in 2020. Three tornadoes would move over this general area in a ten-hour span, the deadliest being the Flat Rock-Trenton EF4.

The tornado maintained EF4 strength as it tore through the rural community of Shiloh, sweeping away numerous mobile homes and block foundation homes and killing five people at that location. Thousands of trees were snapped, a log cabin was destroyed, livestock was killed, chicken houses were flattened, and a van was lofted and dropped into a field 400 yards (370 m) away from where it originated. The tornado then crossed then crossed into Georgia, immediately producing EF4-rated damage west of Workman Drive. As it crossed the road, more EF3 damage was inflicted to a home, which was completely destroyed. It maintained EF3 intensity as it passed over Bible Camp Road; the tornado's outer circulation struck the Vaught Lake area at EF0 to EF2 intensity. On County Road 301, the tornado destroyed another home with wind speeds that were estimated to have been as high as 150 miles per hour (240 km/h). To the northeast the tornado crossed Back Valley Road, where several homes were heavily damaged or destroyed.
The exterior walls of one home were collapsed inward by the tornado as it impacted the Whispering Pines Drive and Tanglewood Trail area. After crossing McKaig Road and Ashton Lane, the tornado impacted Interstate 59 and South Main Street. At this point along its track, the tornado was nearing downtown Trenton. It hit a neighborhood of homes on Pine Avenue, Oak Avenue and Walnut Avenue ease of the State Route; EF2 damage was inflcited to a residence located on Oak Wood Avenue. Dozens of homes in Trenton were either completely destroyed or sustained major damage, and tens of thousands of trees were downed in the area. A grocery store, two apartment complexes, and a funeral home were destroyed as well. The Dade Elementary School was damaged by the tornado, and the tornado left a path of damage that was visible several days after the event.
The tornado weakened to EF2 strength as it struck Flintstone further to the northeast, but still resulted in major damage. Numerous trees and power lines were downed, 7 homes were destroyed, 26 sustained major damage, and 35 sustained minor damage in the Flintstone area. The tornado continued northeast, weakening to EF0 strength before finally dissipating near Fort Oglethorpe. The tornado tracked along a 47-mile-long (76 km) path, at times up to 1,260 yards (1,150 m) wide.


== Aftermath ==


=== Damage, recovery efforts and studies ===

Heavy damage was produced by the tornado in the Sand Mountain region of North Alabama. The Sand Mountain Bible Camp, located near Shiloh, was heavily damaged. Walker County Emergency Management and Walker County Emergency Services cleared debris from roadways and performed search-and-rescue operations in the Flintstone area; four EMA disaster centers were opened by the agency. In Trenton, the tornado resulted in the closure of several stores and businesses. the Trenton Ingles Supermarket remained closed for four months after the tornado, The Moore Funeral Home property was heavily affected by the tornado, although it was later rebuilt. In addition to business damage, several rental properties in Trenton suffered some form of damage from the tornado.
In Jackson County, the tornado impacted Camp Jackson, a child's summer camp. The camp remained closed for several years while repairs were done on the property, and Jackson County itself helped with rebuilding efforts. In DeKalb County, the Disaster Mortuary Operational Response Team worked to identify victims of the tornado and other tornadoes that struck that day.
On January 23, 2025, Anthony W. Lyza with the National Severe Storms Laboratory along with Harold E. Brooks and Makenzie J. Kroca with the University of Oklahoma's School of Meteorology published a paper to the American Meteorological Society, where they stated the tornado in Pisgah was an "EF5 candidate" in relation to the EF5 drought that was ongoing at the time of the paper. The paper was of the opinion that the EF5 starting wind speed should be 190 mph (310 km/h) instead of 201 mph (323 km/h).

On the afternoon of April 27, 2011, a large, long-tracked, and destructive high-end EF4 tornado, known informally as the '''Section–Flat Rock EF4''' by the [[National Weather Service]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Section to Flat Rock EF4 April 27th, 2011 Tornado |url=https://www.weather.gov/hun/4272011_jackson_northern-dekalb |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=[[National Weather Service]] |language=EN-US |archive-date=2025-03-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250328012955/https://www.weather.gov/hun/4272011_jackson_northern-dekalb |url-status=live }}</ref> moved across portions of [[North Alabama]] and [[North Georgia]], tracking near the towns of [[Section, Alabama|Section]], [[Pisgah, Alabama|Pisgah]], [[Flat Rock, Alabama|Flat Rock]], [[Higdon, Alabama|Higdon]] and [[Rosalie, Alabama|Rosalie]] in Alabama and [[Trenton, Georgia|Trenton]] in Georgia along its {{convert|47|mi|km|-long|adj=mid}} track. The tornado directly killed 15 people, injured at least 50 more, and impacted hundreds of structures. It occurred as part of the [[2011 Super Outbreak|largest tornado outbreak in modern history]], and was one of multiple EF4-rated tornadoes to be confirmed that day.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-07-31 |title=Revisiting the April 2011 Tornado “Super Outbreak” from Orbit |url=https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/news/revisiting-the-april-2011-tornado-super-outbreak-orbit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250823223202/https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/news/revisiting-the-april-2011-tornado-super-outbreak-orbit |archive-date=August 23, 2025 |access-date=2025-08-04 |publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] |language=en}}</ref> 

The tornado first touched down near Section, initially producing EF0 and EF1-rated damage to trees and homes before becoming violent north of Pisgah. Several homes were heavily damaged in the area and trees were blown down; the tornado killed 13 people in [[Jackson County, Alabama|Jackson County]] alone. The tornado maintained its intensity as it moved through [[DeKalb County, Alabama|Dekalb County]] before crossing into [[Dade County, Georgia]] at EF4 intensity, where two people would be killed and heavy damage was inflicted to the community of Trenton. The tornado lifted after 56 minutes on the ground. Damage from the tornado was rated EF4 on the [[Enhanced Fujita scale]], and damage surveyors estimated that the tornado had maximum estimated wind speeds of approximately {{Convert|190|mph|km/h}}. [[WDEF-TV]] described the tornado as the "longest-running in our area".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parker |first=Collins |date=2016-04-27 |title=Remembering April 27 Minute by Minute: 4:01 Section-to Trenton-to Flintstone |url=https://www.wdef.com/remembering-april-27-minute-minute-2/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240623052815/https://www.wdef.com/remembering-april-27-minute-minute-2/ |archive-date=June 23, 2024 |access-date=2025-08-06 |website=[[WDEF-TV]] |language=en-US}}</ref> 

== Meteorological synopsis ==
{{Main|2011 Super Outbreak#Meteorological synopsis}}

=== Setup ===
The environmental conditions leading up to the 2011 Super Outbreak were among the "most conducive to violent tornadoes ever documented".<ref name="BAMS">{{cite journal |author=Kevin R. Knupp |display-authors=etal |date=July 2014 |title=Meteorological Overview of the Devastating 27 April 2011 Tornado Outbreak |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society]] |publisher=[[American Meteorological Society]] |volume=95 |issue=7 |pages=1,041–1,062 |bibcode=2014BAMS...95.1041K |doi=10.1175/BAMS-D-11-00229.1 |s2cid=22335326}}</ref> On April 25, a vigorous upper-level [[Shortwave (meteorology)|shortwave trough]] moved into the Southern Plains states.<ref>{{cite report |url=http://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/outlook/archive/2011/day1otlk_20110425_1200.html |title=Apr 25, 2011 0600 UTC Day 1 Convective Outlook |author=Ryan E. Jewell |date=April 25, 2011 |publisher=[[Storm Prediction Center]] |location=[[Norman, Oklahoma]] |accessdate=May 15, 2016}}</ref> Ample instability, low-level moisture, and [[wind shear]] all fueled a significant [[tornado outbreak]] from [[Texas]] to [[Tennessee]]; at least 64 tornadoes touched down on this day.<ref name="BAMS" /> An [[Low-pressure area|area of low pressure]] consolidated over Texas on April 26 and traveled east while the aforementioned shortwave trough traversed the [[Mississippi River|Mississippi]] and [[Ohio River]] valleys.<ref>{{cite report |url=http://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/outlook/archive/2011/day1otlk_20110426_1200.html |title=Apr 26, 2011 0600 UTC Day 1 Convective Outlook |author=Ryan E. Jewell |date=April 26, 2011 |publisher=[[Storm Prediction Center]] |location=[[Norman, Oklahoma]] |accessdate=May 15, 2016}}</ref> Another 50 tornadoes touched down on this day.<ref name="BAMS" /> The multi-day outbreak culminated on April 27 with the most violent day of tornadic activity since the [[1974 Super Outbreak]]. Multiple episodes of tornadic activity ensued with two waves of [[Mesoscale convective system|mesoscale convective systems]] in the morning hours followed by a widespread outbreak of [[Supercell|supercells]] from [[Mississippi]] to [[North Carolina]] during the afternoon into the evening.<ref name="BAMS" />

Tornadic activity on April 27 was precipitated by a 995 [[Bar (unit)|mbar]] ([[Pascal (unit)|hPa]]; 29.39 [[Inches of Mercury|inHg]]) surface low situated over [[Kentucky]] and a deep, negatively tilted (aligned northwest to southeast) trough over [[Arkansas]] and [[Louisiana]]. A strong southwesterly surface jet intersected these systems at a 60° angle, an [[Ageostrophy|ageostrophic flow]] that led to [[Hydrodynamical helicity#Meteorology|storm-relative helicity]] values in excess of 500 m<sup>2</sup>s<sup>−2</sup>—indicative of extreme wind shear and a very high potential for rotating [[Vertical draft|updrafts]] within supercells. Ample moisture from the [[Gulf of Mexico]] was brought north across the [[Deep South]], leading to daytime high temperatures of {{convert|25|to|27|C|abbr=on|order=flip|F}} and [[Dewpoint|dewpoints]] of {{convert|19|to|22|C|abbr=on|order=flip|F}}. Furthermore, [[convective available potential energy]] (CAPE) values reached 2,500–3,000 J/kg<sup>−1</sup>.<ref name="BAMS" />

On the morning of April 27, a strong [[cold front]] with several areas of embedded [[Low-pressure area|low pressure]] extended from the [[Texas Hill Country]] northeastward towards the [[Ark-La-Tex|Arklatex]] and the [[Ozarks]], and later into the lower [[Ohio River|Ohio Valley]]. Warm moist air was in place due to strong southerly flow ahead of the front over Mississippi, Alabama, and Tennessee. An upper level disturbance sparked a broad area of [[Rain|showers]] and [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]] as it moved across the frontal boundary on the previous evening. The eastern edge of the line of showers and storms continued to move eastward, in concert with the upper disturbance, reaching the northwest Alabama border around 2:00 a.m. CDT.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Weather Setup: April 27th, 2011 Historic Tornado Outbreak |url=https://www.weather.gov/hun/hunsur_2011-04-27_setup |access-date=2024-11-07 |publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] |language=EN-US |archive-date=2024-11-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241108220517/https://www.weather.gov/hun/hunsur_2011-04-27_setup |url-status=live }} {{source-attribution}}</ref>

This produced the last and most violent round of severe weather, which began around 2:30 p.m. CDT for northern Alabama as supercells began to line up to the southwest of the area. During the early afternoon hours, the potential for destructive tornadoes was highlighted by the [[Storm Prediction Center]]'s upgrade to a [[List of Storm Prediction Center high risk days|high risk]] for severe weather around 1:00 p.m. CDT.<ref name=":3" /> This prompted a [[particularly dangerous situation]] (PDS) [[tornado watch]], which was issued for northern Alabama and portions of southern [[Tennessee]] at 1:45 p.m. CDT. The bulletin that accompanied the watch read:<ref>{{Cite web |last=Center |first=Storm Prediction |title=Storm Prediction Center Tornado/Severe Thunderstorm Watch Page |url=https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/watch/2011/ww0235.html |access-date=2024-11-07 |website=[[Storm Prediction Center]] |language=EN-US |archive-date=2024-12-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204013839/https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/watch/2011/ww0235.html |url-status=live }}</ref>
{{Blockquote|text=THE NWS STORM PREDICTION CENTER HAS ISSUED A TORNADO WATCH FOR PORTIONS OF: MUCH OF ALABAMA, NORTHWEST GEORGIA, SOUTHEAST MISSISSIPPI, SOUTHERN MIDDLE TENNESSEE, EFFECTIVE THIS WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON AND EVENING FROM 145 PM UNTIL 1000 PM CDT.
   
{{red|...THIS IS A PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS SITUATION...}}
   
DESTRUCTIVE TORNADOES...LARGE HAIL TO 4 INCHES IN DIAMETER. THUNDERSTORM WIND GUSTS TO 80 MPH...AND DANGEROUS LIGHTNING ARE POSSIBLE IN THESE AREAS.}}
The potential for tornadoes ramped up from noon through 9:00 p.m. CDT. During this period, much of Alabama experienced numerous [[Supercell|supercell thunderstorms]] that produced numerous tornadoes, including the Trenton tornado.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Morgan |first=Leigh |date=2022-04-27 |title=18 hours of horror: A look back at the tornadoes of April 27, 2011 |url=https://www.al.com/news/2022/04/18-hours-of-horror-a-look-back-at-the-tornadoes-of-april-27-2011.html |access-date=2024-11-07 |website=[[Al.com]] |language=en |archive-date=2024-11-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241108214740/https://www.al.com/news/2022/04/18-hours-of-horror-a-look-back-at-the-tornadoes-of-april-27-2011.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-11-25 |title=Remembering April 27, 2011 in photos |url=https://www.wvtm13.com/article/remembering-april-27-2011-in-photos/3827940 |access-date=November 7, 2024 |publisher=[[WVTM]] |language=en |archive-date=December 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203180226/https://www.wvtm13.com/article/remembering-april-27-2011-in-photos/3827940 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Morning EF1 tornado in Trenton and New England, Georgia ===
On the morning of April 27, an EF1 tornado touched down a short distance to the north of where the EF4 tornado would later impact. The tornado touched down at around 8:40 a.m. CDT on top of an interchange in the western portions, moving to the northeast. West of Wolverine Drive the tornado reached EF1 intensity, impacting the Dade Elementary before crossing 1st Street and John Street. It weakened to EF0 strength shortly before passing over Wren Avenue. The tornado moved through a neighborhood between North Main Street and [[Interstate 59 in Georgia|Interstate 59]] before moving directly parallel to Highway 11. It reached EF1 intensity for a second  time as it impacted the northwest portions of [[New England, Georgia|New England]], before weakening again as it crossed Squirrel Town Creek.<ref name=":4" /> The tornado continued northeast through unpopulated areas in Dade County to the west of [[Morganville, Georgia|Morganville]]. It remained relatively thin as it moved over the Slygo Ridge, part of the [[Slygo Valley]] region. Several roads were hit at EF0 intensity as the tornado continued, eventually crossing [[Interstate 24]] and lifting a short distance to the west of [[Hooker, Georgia|Hooker]]. The tornado caused no fatalities or injuries.<ref name=":4" />

== Tornado summary ==

This multiple-vortex EF4 tornado that originated from the Cullman supercell, with maximum sustained winds of up to {{convert|190|mph|km/h|abbr=on}}, devastated portions of [[Jackson County, Alabama|Jackson]] and [[DeKalb County, Alabama|DeKalb]] counties in Alabama, as well as [[Dade County, Georgia|Dade]] and [[Walker County, Georgia|Walker]] counties in Georgia along a {{convert|47|mi|km|-long|adj=mid}} path at times up to {{convert|1260|yd|m}} wide, killing 14 people and injuring at least 50 others.<ref name="Storm Events Database">{{cite web |title=Storm Events Database |url=http://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/stormevents/eventdetails.jsp?id=304631 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714204452/http://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/stormevents/eventdetails.jsp?id=304631 |archive-date=July 14, 2014 |access-date=June 15, 2014 |website=[[National Climatic Data Center]]}}</ref><ref name="ncdc.noaa.gov">{{cite web |title=Storm Events Database |url=http://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/stormevents/eventdetails.jsp?id=304667 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714201631/http://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/stormevents/eventdetails.jsp?id=304667 |archive-date=July 14, 2014 |access-date=June 15, 2014 |website=[[National Climatic Data Center]]}}</ref>
[[File:Damage to homes in Jackson County, Alabama following a devastating EF4 tornado 01.jpg|thumb|Damage to homes in Jackson County|alt=A road with damaged structures lining its sides.]]
The tornado first touched down on Alabama State Highway 35, moving to the northeast. It moved parallel to County Road 390, before crossing over Alabama State Highway 40. Trees were blown down north of County Road 224,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=April 2011 Tornado Response Imagery |url=https://geodesy.noaa.gov/storm_archive/storms/apr11_tornado/index.html |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]]}}</ref> before the tornado briefly moved over an offshoot of the Tennessee River. It continued moving northeast through hilly areas of Marshall County, continuing to produce tree damage and damaging several homes near County Road 88.<ref name=":0" /> Off Alabama State Highway 88, several homes sustained damage and trees were blown down on the properties. The tornado then crossed County Road 432 and County Road 57, impacting the Dogwood Branch of the Tennessee River directly north of Pisgah. On County Roads 369, several homes were heavily damaged.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />

To their north the tornado tossed debris into a grove of trees and scattered debris from a property across a field. The tornado then passed over County Road 58 and County Road 357, where more damage was done to trees and homes. A home was destroyed as the tornado passed over County Road 58 before the tornado crossed over the Rocky Branch of the Tennessee River. It then impacted County Road 426 and County Road 126 north of the communities of Glenzaida and [[Rosalie, Alabama|Rosalie]]. The tornado continued moving through areas a short distance south of the Coon Gulf and northwest to north of County Road 78. The tornado rapidly intensified to low-end EF4 strength in this area as it destroyed numerous mobile homes and brick-foundation homes, scattering debris hundreds of yards and killing three people.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Damage Assessment Toolkit |url=https://apps.dat.noaa.gov/StormDamage/DamageViewer/ |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] |archive-date=2020-04-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200423095631/https://apps.dat.noaa.gov/stormdamage/damageviewer/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
[[File:Aerial of Trenton, Georgia following an EF4 tornado on April 27, 2011.png|left|thumb|271x271px|Aerial photograph of Trenton, Georgia on May 4, showing damaged homes|alt=An aerial view of a town, showing several damaged homes along a grid of streets.]]
Thousands of trees were snapped and debarked, vehicles were thrown up to {{convert|50|yd|m}} in different directions, and barns and chicken houses were heavily damaged, along with the roof of a church.<ref name="NOAA">{{cite web |date=February 15, 2012 |title=Eastern Jackson (AL) / Northern De kalb (AL) - EF-4 (Section to Flat Rock to GA) |url=http://www.srh.noaa.gov/hun/?n=04272011_jackson_northern-dekalb |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131229063904/http://www.srh.noaa.gov/hun/?n=04272011_jackson_northern-dekalb |archive-date=December 29, 2013 |access-date=June 15, 2014 |publisher=[[National Weather Service]] office in [[Huntsville, Alabama]]. [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]]}}</ref> As it passed near [[Flat Rock, Alabama|Flat Rock]] and [[Higdon, Alabama|Higdon]], the tornado reached high-end EF4 strength, mowing down thousands of trees in this rural area. As the tornado struck a farm, a home and two chicken houses were completely obliterated and swept away. A heavy propane tank was lofted and thrown {{convert|100|yd|m}} from one of the chicken houses, and 19 cattle on the property were killed. Remarkably, a family of four taking shelter inside the house were completely unharmed.<ref name="NOAA" /> Three people were killed in a home southwest of Flat Rock.<ref>{{Cite news |title=EF4 tornado on Apr. 27, 2011 15:01 PM CDT |url=https://data.montgomeryadvertiser.com/tornado-archive/alabama/301925/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230522230125/https://data.montgomeryadvertiser.com/tornado-archive/alabama/301925/ |archive-date=2023-05-22 |access-date=2025-08-06 |work=[[The Montgomery Advertiser]] |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> The Shiloh Community Church in the Higdon area was hit by the tornado; the same church would be struck by another tornado in 2020.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lP-T3CdSUzA |title=Church in Alabama hit by 2011 and 2020 tornadoes |date=2020-04-19 |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=[[Local 3 News]] |via=[[YouTube]]}}</ref> Three tornadoes would move over this general area in a ten-hour span, the deadliest being the Flat Rock-Trenton EF4.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-05-01 |title=Alabama family struck twice by deadly tornadoes; 'it came back ... and it killed more' |url=https://www.al.com/wire/2011/05/alabama_family_struck_twice_by.html |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=[[Associated Press]] |language=en}}</ref>
[[File:Track and intensity map of the April 27, 2011 Flat Rock, AL tornado through Trenton, GA.png|thumb|Track and intensity map of the tornado through Trenton, Georgia{{Efn|The damage path to the north indicates the track of an EF1 tornado that hit Trenton on the morning of April 27 as part of a morning round of severe storms.}}{{divhide|Key}}

The tornado maintained EF4 strength as it tore through the rural community of Shiloh, sweeping away numerous mobile homes and block foundation homes and killing five people at that location. Thousands of trees were snapped, a log cabin was destroyed, livestock was killed, chicken houses were flattened, and a van was lofted and dropped into a field {{convert|400|yd|m}} away from where it originated.<ref name="NOAA" /> The tornado then crossed then crossed into Georgia, immediately producing EF4-rated damage west of Workman Drive. As it crossed the road, more EF3 damage was inflicted to a home, which was completely destroyed. It maintained EF3 intensity as it passed over Bible Camp Road; the tornado's outer circulation struck the Vaught Lake area at EF0 to EF2 intensity. On County Road 301, the tornado destroyed another home with wind speeds that were estimated to have been as high as {{Convert|150|mph|km/h}}. To the northeast the tornado crossed Back Valley Road, where several homes were heavily damaged or destroyed.<ref name=":4" />

The exterior walls of one home were collapsed inward by the tornado as it impacted the Whispering Pines Drive and Tanglewood Trail area. After crossing McKaig Road and Ashton Lane, the tornado impacted Interstate 59 and South Main Street. At this point along its track, the tornado was nearing downtown Trenton. It hit a neighborhood of homes on Pine Avenue, Oak Avenue and Walnut Avenue ease of the State Route; EF2 damage was inflcited to a residence located on Oak Wood Avenue. Dozens of homes in Trenton were either completely destroyed or sustained major damage, and tens of thousands of trees were downed in the area. A grocery store, two apartment complexes, and a funeral home were destroyed as well.<ref name="Storm Events Database" /> The Dade Elementary School was damaged by the tornado,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Community Remembers April 27th Tornados As 10th Anniversary Of Outbreak Approaches |url=https://www.dadecountysentinel.com/2021/04/22/community-remembers-april-27th-tornados-as-10th-anniversary-of-outbreak-approaches/ |access-date=2025-08-06 |website=Dade County Sentinel |language=en-US}}</ref> and the tornado left a path of damage that was visible several days after the event.<ref name=":0" />

The tornado weakened to EF2 strength as it struck [[Flintstone, Georgia|Flintstone]] further to the northeast,<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2021-04-28 |title=10 Years after the Super Outbreak Impacted Walker County |url=https://walkercountyga.gov/2021/04/28/10-years-after-the-super-outbreak-impacted-walker-county/ |access-date=2025-08-06 |website=Walker County, GA (.gov) |language=en-US}}</ref> but still resulted in major damage. Numerous trees and power lines were downed, 7 homes were destroyed, 26 sustained major damage, and 35 sustained minor damage in the Flintstone area. The tornado continued northeast, weakening to EF0 strength before finally dissipating near [[Fort Oglethorpe, Georgia|Fort Oglethorpe]].<ref name="ncdc.noaa.gov" /> The tornado tracked along a {{convert|47|mi|km|-long|adj=mid}} path, at times up to {{convert|1260|yd|m}} wide.<ref name="Storm Events Database" /><ref name="ncdc.noaa.gov" />

== Aftermath ==

=== Damage, recovery efforts and studies ===
[[File:Damage to Camp Jackson in Jackson County, Alabama following an EF4 tornado on April 27, 2011.png|thumb|Camp Jackson, located in Jackson County, was heavily damaged by the tornado|alt=An aerial view of a forested area with a few buildings, showing trees blown down along a lakeshore.]]
Heavy damage was produced by the tornado in the [[Sand Mountain (Alabama)|Sand Mountain]] region of North Alabama. The Sand Mountain Bible Camp, located near Shiloh, was heavily damaged.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-05-03 |title=Sand Mt. Bible Camp & others need help |url=https://tristateibpf.org/2011/05/03/sand-mt-bible-camp-others-need-help/ |access-date=2025-08-06 |publisher=Tri-State Independent Baptist Preachers Fellowship |language=en-US |archive-date=2025-03-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250316194618/https://tristateibpf.org/2011/05/03/sand-mt-bible-camp-others-need-help/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Walker County Emergency Management and Walker County Emergency Services cleared debris from roadways and performed search-and-rescue operations in the Flintstone area; four EMA disaster centers were opened by the agency.<ref name=":2" /> In Trenton, the tornado resulted in the closure of several stores and businesses. the Trenton Ingles Supermarket remained closed for four months after the tornado,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Carroll |first=David |date=2011-08-31 |title=Ingles re-opens Trenton store 4 months after tornado |url=https://www.local3news.com/ingles-re-opens-trenton-store-4-months-after-tornado/article_c77c910e-8430-50df-90c0-dd9b4352196c.html |access-date=2025-08-06 |website=Local3News |language=en}}</ref> The Moore Funeral Home property was heavily affected by the tornado, although it was later rebuilt.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Moore Funeral Homes |url=https://www.moorefhs.com/about-us |access-date=2025-08-06 |website=Moore FHS |language=en |archive-date=2025-07-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250722060515/https://www.moorefhs.com/about-us |url-status=live }}</ref> In addition to business damage, several rental properties in Trenton suffered some form of damage from the tornado.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Glover |first=Greg |date=2011-07-08 |title=Trenton lost rental properties in tornadoes, rebuilding is slow |url=https://www.local3news.com/trenton-lost-rental-properties-in-tornadoes-rebuilding-is-slow/article_1c4b2730-9e8d-5818-862e-7312dc600aa2.html |access-date=2025-08-06 |website=Local3News |language=en}}</ref>

In Jackson County, the tornado impacted Camp Jackson, a child's summer camp. The camp remained closed for several years while repairs were done on the property, and Jackson County itself helped with rebuilding efforts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 1, 2014 |title=Jackson County aims to help repair Camp Jackson |url=https://whnt.com/news/northeast-alabama/jackson-county-aims-to-help-repair-camp-jackson/ |access-date=August 6, 2025 |website=[[WHNT]]}}</ref> In DeKalb County, the Disaster Mortuary Operational Response Team worked to identify victims of the tornado and other tornadoes that struck that day.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Lisa |title=Disaster team helps deal with mass fatalities in DeKalb County |url=https://www.gadsdentimes.com/story/news/local/2011/04/29/disaster-team-helps-deal-with-mass-fatalities-in-dekalb-county/32149941007/ |access-date=2025-08-06 |website=[[Gadsden Times]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

On January 23, 2025, [[Anthony Lyza|Anthony W. Lyza]] with the [[National Severe Storms Laboratory]] along with Harold E. Brooks and Makenzie J. Kroca with the [[University of Oklahoma]]'s School of Meteorology published a paper to the [[American Meteorological Society]], where they stated the tornado in Pisgah was an "EF5 candidate" in relation to the [[EF5 drought]] that was ongoing at the time of the paper. The paper was of the opinion that the EF5 starting wind speed should be {{convert|190|mph|km/h|abbr=on}} instead of {{convert|201|mph|km/h|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Lyza2025">{{cite journal |last1=Lyza |first1=Anthony W. |author-link=Anthony Lyza |last2=Brooks |first2=Harold E. |last3=Krocak |first3=Makenzie J. |date=23 January 2025 |title=Where Have the EF5s Gone? A Closer Look at the “Drought” of the Most Violent Tornadoes in the United States |url=https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/bams/aop/BAMS-D-24-0066.1/BAMS-D-24-0066.1.xml |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society]] |publisher=[[American Meteorological Society]] |doi=10.1175/BAMS-D-24-0066.1 |url-access=subscription |access-date=2 February 2025 |archive-date=13 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250213185416/https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/bams/aop/BAMS-D-24-0066.1/BAMS-D-24-0066.1.xml |url-status=live }}</ref>
